summary.text: Take the composite number \(n=23492890653051=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\).  Using multiplicativity of the gcd-sum and its value \(2p-1\) at a prime gives \(\sum_{k=1}^n\gcd(k,n)=610815156979325\), whose successor is \(26n\); hence the relevant gcd equals \(n\) and the resulting value is \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd\!\left(n,1+\sum_{k=1}^n\gcd(k,n)\right)}.
\]
We will exhibit a composite positive integer \(n\neq 1\) for which \(A(n)=1\).

The counterexample is
\[
n=23492890653051=3\cdot 37\cdot 43\cdot 42307\cdot 116341.
\]
We first justify the primality facts used in evaluating the gcd-sum, then derive the relevant gcd-sum formula and carry out the numerical calculation.

### 1. Primality of the factors

The numbers \(3,37,43\) are prime by trial division: for \(37\) and \(43\), it is enough to test the primes \(2,3,5\), since their square roots are less than \(7\).

For completeness, the two larger factors can be proved prime using Lucas's primality criterion. We use the following standard form of that criterion: if \(N>1\), the complete prime factorization of \(N-1\) is known, and there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{N-1}\equiv 1\pmod N
\]
and, for every distinct prime \(q\mid N-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(N-1)/q}-1,N\bigr)=1,
\]
then \(N\) is prime. Indeed, for every prime divisor \(r\) of \(N\), the order of \(b\) modulo \(r\) divides \(N-1\). The gcd conditions force that order to contain the full prime-power contribution of every prime dividing \(N-1\), so the order is exactly divisible by \(N-1\). Hence \(N-1\mid r-1\), which forces \(r\ge N\). Since \(r\mid N\), it follows that \(r=N\), and thus \(N\) is prime.

For \(42307\), we have the complete factorization
\[
42307-1=42306=2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641.
\]
The number \(641\) is prime: since \(25^2<641<26^2\), it suffices to test divisibility by
\(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\), and division by each gives a nonzero remainder. Using the base \(b=3\), repeated-squaring modular exponentiation gives
\[
3^{42306}\equiv1\pmod{42307},
\]
and the following table gives the residues needed for the four distinct prime divisors of \(42306\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&3^{42306/q}\bmod 42307&
\gcd(3^{42306/q}-1,42307)\\ \hline
2&42306&1\\
3&36715&1\\
11&17937&1\\
641&10961&1
\end{array}
\]
The gcds in the final column follow directly from the Euclidean algorithm applied to one less than each displayed residue and \(42307\). Lucas's criterion therefore proves that \(42307\) is prime.

Similarly,
\[
116341-1=116340=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\]
The number \(277\) is prime: because \(16^2<277<17^2\), one only needs to test the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), none of which divides \(277\). With base \(b=14\), modular exponentiation gives
\[
14^{116340}\equiv1\pmod{116341},
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&14^{116340/q}\bmod 116341&
\gcd(14^{116340/q}-1,116341)\\ \hline
2&116340&1\\
3&50801&1\\
5&81650&1\\
7&10889&1\\
277&35125&1
\end{array}
\]
Again, the last column is obtained by the Euclidean algorithm. Lucas's criterion proves that \(116341\) is prime.

Thus all five displayed factors of \(n\) are distinct primes. Their product is checked successively as follows:
\[
3\cdot37=111,
\]
\[
111\cdot43=4773,
\]
\[
4773\cdot42307=201931311,
\]
\[
201931311\cdot116341=23492890653051.
\]
In particular, \(n\) is composite; for example, it is divisible by \(3\) and is larger than \(3\). It is also plainly not equal to \(1\).

### 2. Evaluation of the gcd-sum

Define
\[
G(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n\gcd(k,n).
\]
We use the divisor formula
\[
G(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d),                       \tag{1}
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function.

To prove (1), group the integers \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) according to the value \(d=\gcd(k,n)\). If \(d\mid n\), write \(k=dm\). Then
\[
\gcd(k,n)=d
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gcd(m,n/d)=1.
\]
As \(k\) ranges from \(1\) to \(n\), the corresponding \(m\) ranges from \(1\) to \(n/d\). Exactly \(\varphi(n/d)\) of those values are relatively prime to \(n/d\). Thus there are \(\varphi(n/d)\) terms whose gcd with \(n\) equals \(d\), and each contributes \(d\). Summing over all divisors \(d\) proves (1).

The function \(G\) is multiplicative: if \(u\) and \(v\) are coprime, then
\[
G(uv)=G(u)G(v).                                             \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, every divisor of \(uv\) has a unique form \(d_1d_2\) with \(d_1\mid u\) and \(d_2\mid v\). Moreover, \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) are coprime, as are \(u/d_1\) and \(v/d_2\), so multiplicativity of Euler's totient gives
\[
\varphi\left(\frac{uv}{d_1d_2}\right)
 =\varphi(u/d_1)\varphi(v/d_2).
\]
Substituting this into (1) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(uv)
&=\sum_{d_1\mid u}\sum_{d_2\mid v}
 d_1d_2\,\varphi(u/d_1)\varphi(v/d_2)\\
&=\left(\sum_{d_1\mid u}d_1\varphi(u/d_1)\right)
  \left(\sum_{d_2\mid v}d_2\varphi(v/d_2)\right)\\
&=G(u)G(v),
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (2).

For a prime \(p\), formula (1) has only the two divisors \(1,p\), and therefore
\[
G(p)=1\cdot\varphi(p)+p\cdot\varphi(1)
=(p-1)+p=2p-1.                                             \tag{3}
\]
Since the five prime factors of our \(n\) are distinct and hence pairwise coprime, repeated application of (2) and (3) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(n)
&=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
  (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
&=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
The product can be checked in stages:
\[
5\cdot73=365,
\qquad
365\cdot85=31025,
\]
\[
31025\cdot84613=2625118325,
\]
and
\[
2625118325\cdot232681=610815156979325.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{23492890653051}\gcd(k,23492890653051)
=610815156979325.                                          \tag{4}
\]

### 3. The value of the sequence at the counterexample

Adding \(1\) to the value in (4) gives
\[
1+G(n)=610815156979326.
\]
But direct multiplication shows
\[
610815156979326
=26\cdot23492890653051
=26n.
\]
Therefore
\[
\gcd(n,1+G(n))=\gcd(n,26n)=n,
\]
because \(n>0\). It follows that
\[
A(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+G(n))}= rac{n}{n}=1.
\]

We have thus found
\[
n=23492890653051

to be a positive composite integer, different from \(1\), for which \(A(n)=1\). Hence the assertion that \(A(n)=1\) holds if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime is false.
